title: The Divine Office
hookLine: monks stop whatever they're doing to pray at set hours, day and night

lines: EVERYTHING ELSE FITS IN THE GAPS.
cards: Deep in the night, a bell rings in a monastery. Doors open along a dark corridor. Men in robes walk to the church, some still blinking, and begin to sing psalms.
A few hours later, at first light, the bell again. Early morning, again. Midmorning.
And once more before sleep. A brother could be kneading bread, halfway through a sentence in a book, or up a ladder fixing a gutter. When the bell rings, he stops.

teach.h: A VERSE: SEVEN TIMES A DAY.
teach.b: The Divine Office is the round of prayer at set hours, made mostly of psalms, that Christian monks, and others too, keep through the day and night. First, a verse.
The Psalms speak of praying by the clock: "Seven times a day do I praise thee because of thy righteous judgments." And: "At midnight I will rise to give thanks unto thee." Second, a rule.

teach.h: A RULE: BENEDICT SETS THE HOURS.
teach.b: Benedict of Nursia, whose Rule you met on day eight hundred ninety, wrote it for monks, and it is still followed in monasteries today.

He takes those two verses at their word: seven times in the day he sets an hour of prayer, and once in the night, the night office. In his rule, all the psalms are sung through each week. Third, the bell.

teach.h: THE BELL: PUT IT DOWN AND COME.
teach.b: When the signal for prayer sounds, Benedict says, a monk should put down whatever is in his hands and come at once, though calmly, without rushing about.
He calls the prayer the work of God, and says nothing is to be put before it.
Fourth, beyond the monastery. Catholics call it the Liturgy of the Hours, and priests, religious and lay people pray it. Anglicans pray Morning and Evening Prayer from the Book of Common Prayer.

teach.h: SEVEN TIMES A DAY DO I PRAISE THEE.
teach.b: Orthodox Christians keep their own cycle of hours. This week brought a scene stepped into, a castle, a dark night, one sacred word, shared silence, a sung line: ways to pray.
The Office is a way to keep praying, by giving the day a skeleton and hanging everything else on it.

how: Monks and nuns gather in church at set hours to sing psalms and prayers; Catholics also pray the Liturgy of the Hours from a breviary or app, and Anglicans pray Morning and Evening Prayer from the Book of Common Prayer.

games.q: you're a monk halfway through kneading bread when the bell for prayer rings. what does Benedict's rule say to do?
o: finish the bread, then come to pray.
put it down and come at once, calmly.
pray where you are, since work is prayer too.
games.why: Benedict says to set down whatever is in your hands and come at once, though without rushing about. nothing is to be put before the work of God.

practice: Put down whatever is in your hands and let them rest, as if this sit were the first of three set hours in your day.
If you pray, you can say a line from a psalm you know; if not, breathe and notice the hour: the light in the room, the sounds, what this part of the day is like.

wordCard.voice: The Divine Office. The round of psalms and prayers kept at set hours of the day and night, which Benedict called the work of God. Today's word.

orig.note: Latin: the work of God. Benedict's name in his rule for the hours of prayer.
